sweep_summary: Ngbaka Minagende is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword hit (Laks 2009, Hebrew prosodic templates) is a Glottolog computerized mis-assignment ('choose' -> nga) and is irrelevant.org: Bible, Swadesh list, Wikipedia only; HathiTrust 403; Google Books 403/API 429; The best statement read, verified against the page image we hold, is Moñino 1995 p. 285 Remarque 2: none of the 21 Gbaya languages, Ngbaka-minagende included, has any accent, intensity or length phenomenon -- i.e. tone only, no word stress -- but it is second-hand (from Maes 1959/1968). Tucker & Bryan 1966 §2b only notes penultimate extra shortness for 'NGBAKA' (ambiguous with Ngbaka Ma'bo). Highest acquisition priority: Maes 1959 (Harvard print, a library scan; index hits for 'accent dynamique' pp. 11-12), then Henrix et al. 2007 and Grand'Eury 1991/1987.

new_statements.translation: [p.285] Remark 2. To the question raised by Jacqueline Thomas, whether the differences in tonal treatment according to syllable type might be explained by the presence of an accent in the languages concerned, the answer must be negative: none of them currently shows any phenomenon of accent, intensity or length. The hypothesis will be raised again diachronically, when interpreting the sound correspondences (p. 345). [p.345] The absence of accent in the present-day languages does not impose this solution for Proto-Gbaya, but the hypothesis can be entertained for an earlier stage of the evolution.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Three-level tone language (H, M, L plus falling and rising contours; every vowel tone-bearing); according to Moñino the present-day Gbaya-Manza-Ngbaka languages, Ngbaka-Minagende among the 21 surveyed, have no accent, no intensity prominence and no length. This is a family-level generalisation; Moñino's Ngbaka-Minagende data are second-hand (Maes 1959, 1968), and Maes 1959 pp. 11-12 contain an unread passage on 'accent dynamique'.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Note the p.285 sentence is made in the context of the 'aire a' Gbaya varieties with syllable-sensitive tone sandhi (Ngbaka is in 'aire b'); the p.345 sentence ('les langues actuelles') is general. Tucker & Bryan 1966 mention only a 'tendency towards extra shortness' of the penultimate in 'NGBAKA, GBAYA, BANDA' (which Ngbaka unclear).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prosody in a comparative phonological survey; no discussion of phrase-level prominence or citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Target is Ngbaka Minagende [nga] (Gbaya-Manza-Ngbaka), not Ngbaka Ma'bo [nbm, ngba1284] (Thomas 1963 'Le parler ngbaka de Bokanga', van de Weijer 1994) nor Ngbaka Manza [ngg, ngba1287] (Selezilo 2008). Moñino's chapter rests on Maes 1959/1968 = western dialect (west and south of Gemena); Grand'Eury 1987/1991 describe the eastern parler; Maes 1945 says the two dialects differ little and are mutually intelligible. Tucker & Bryan's bare 'NGBAKA' in their stress remark is ambiguous between the two Ngbakas.

new_statements.translation: To the question, raised by Jacqueline Thomas, whether the differences in tonal treatment according to syllable type could be explained by the presence of an accent in the languages concerned, the answer must be negative: none of them currently shows any phenomenon of accent, intensity or length.
new_statements.citation: Moñino, Yves (1995). Le proto-gbaya: essai de linguistique comparative historique sur vingt-et-une langues d'Afrique centrale. Paris: Peeters (SELAF 357).
new_statements.locator: p. 285, Récapitulation contrastive, Remarque 2 (Ngbaka-minagende chapter pp. 228-241 is based on Maes 1959/1968, p. 228)
new_statements.reading: No word stress/accent in Ngbaka Minagende (nor in any of the 21 Gbaya languages surveyed); word prosody is tonal only (H, M, L plus falling and rising, p. 229). Caveat: for Ngbaka-minagende Moñino works from Maes 1959/1968, not his own fieldwork, and the unread Maes 1959 sketch reportedly mentions an 'accent dynamique' (pp. 11-12), so this statement is the best read but not the last word.

sources.quote: 2b. Stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length. In MAYOGO there is a tendency towards vowel length on the penultimate syllable. In NGBAKA, GBAYA, and BANDA, on the other hand, there is a tendency towards extra shortness here.
sources.note: Areal remark, not a placement rule: says stress affects vowel quality/length and that in NGBAKA, GBAYA and BANDA there is a tendency to extra shortness on the penultimate syllable. Bare 'NGBAKA' is ambiguous between Ngbaka Ma'bo (their source Thomas 1963) and Ngbaka Gbaya = Ngbaka Minagende; no statement of where word stress falls.
